top_level_objectives: Define a vector as a mathematical object with both magnitude and direction.
Decompose a 2D vector into its perpendicular x and y components using trigonometric principles.
Perform vector addition graphically using the tip-to-tail method.
Relate abstract vector components to the initial horizontal and vertical velocities of a launched projectile.
Analyze the motion of a projectile to conclude that horizontal velocity is constant while vertical velocity changes due to gravity (independence of motion).
Predict and observe how varying initial launch angle and speed alters a projectile's parabolic trajectory, maximum height, and range.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the fundamental properties of vectors, specifically magnitude and direction, in a tangible AR space.
key_visuals: A large, glowing 3D arrow (vector) floating above the workspace.
A dynamic text panel displaying the current magnitude (length) and direction (angle) of the vector.
A visual grid projected onto the floor to provide spatial reference.
student_actions: Grab the tip of the vector and drag it to change its length and orientation.
Observe how the live readout of magnitude and angle updates in real-time as the vector is manipulated.

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate how a single vector can be decomposed into perpendicular horizontal (x) and vertical (y) components using right-triangle trigonometry.
key_visuals: The original main vector, now with dotted projection lines dropping to the x and y axes.
Two new component vectors (e.g., blue for x, red for y) lying along the axes.
Floating holographic equations showing the trigonometric relationships (Vx = V * cos(theta), Vy = V * sin(theta)).
student_actions: Manipulate the main vector's angle and observe the x and y component vectors grow and shrink inversely.
Toggle a 'triangle view' that moves the y-component to the tip of the x-component to explicitly form a right triangle.
Match given magnitude/angle values to achieve target x and y components.

scenes.brief_purpose: Teach the tip-to-tail method of vector addition and how components sum together.
key_visuals: Two distinct interactive vectors (Vector A and Vector B) originating from the same point.
A 'Resultant' vector (Vector C) in a distinct color (e.g., green).
Grid snapping points to help align vectors.
student_actions: Grab Vector B and translate its tail to the tip of Vector A.
Watch the Resultant vector automatically draw from the tail of A to the tip of B.
Examine the component breakdown panel to verify that Cx = Ax + Bx and Cy = Ay + By.

scenes.brief_purpose: Bridge the abstract mathematics of vectors to the physical phenomenon of projectile motion.
key_visuals: A stylized 3D cannon sitting on the floor or table.
An initial velocity vector (v0) protruding from the cannon's barrel, visually split into horizontal (v0x) and vertical (v0y) components.
Dials for adjusting launch speed and launch angle.
student_actions: Turn the cannon's angle dial to raise and lower the barrel.
Observe how changing the angle redistributes the initial velocity between the x and y components before firing.
Fire a test projectile and watch the velocity vector travel with it.

scenes.scene_name: Scene 5: Independence of Motion in Flight
scenes.brief_purpose: Visualize the independence of horizontal and vertical motion during a projectile's flight.
key_visuals: A projectile moving along a parabolic trajectory in slow-motion.
Live velocity component vectors (Vx and Vy) attached to the projectile during flight.
A timeline slider to scrub back and forth through the trajectory.
student_actions: Fire the cannon and pause the projectile mid-flight.
Scrub through the timeline to observe that the horizontal vector (Vx) remains perfectly constant in length.
Observe the vertical vector (Vy) shrink on the way up, disappear at the apex, and grow in the opposite direction on the way down.

scenes.brief_purpose: Investigate how launch parameters (angle and speed) affect the macro properties of the trajectory: range and maximum height.
key_visuals: The cannon setup, now with persistent glowing trails left behind by previous shots.
Target landing zones and a physical 'measuring tape' on the ground.
Floating markers indicating the apex (maximum height) of each trajectory.
student_actions: Keep the speed constant and fire projectiles at 30, 45, and 60 degrees.
Compare the glowing parabolic trails to conclude which angle yields the maximum range (45 degrees) and which yield the same range (complementary angles 30 and 60).
Adjust the launch speed to hit a specific randomized target placed on the floor.
